title: Inside the Cell
subject: biology
author: Clueberry Desk
introduction: A short walk around the smallest working room in biology.

entries.clue: Catalyst whose name usually ends in -ase
entries.explanation: Lactase, amylase, protease — the suffix is a naming convention agreed in the 1890s.
In eukaryotes the chromosomes sit inside a double-membraned compartment.
An acidic sac full of digestive enzymes that breaks down worn-out parts.
The eardrum is the tympanic version; cells are wrapped in a lipid one.

entries.clue: Camillo who lent his name to an apparatus
entries.explanation: Camillo Golgi described the stacked structure in 1898.
entries.sourceNotes: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1906.

entries.clue: Water tank in a plant cell

entries.explanation: Adenosine triphosphate, textbook shorthand for stored chemical energy.

entries.clue: Tiny oars on a cell surface
entries.explanation: Hair-like projections that beat in coordinated waves to move fluid or the cell itself.

factCards.text: Camillo Golgi shared the 1906 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Santiago Ramón y Cajal for their work on the structure of the nervous system.
factCards.sourceTitle: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1906

factCards.text: Ribosomes appear in every known living cell, including bacteria, which have no nucleus at all.
factCards.sourceTitle: Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell

factCards.text: The central vacuole can take up most of the volume of a mature plant cell, and the water pressure inside it helps keep leaves and stems rigid.
